inputs.need:
I am the lead physiotherapist for a hospital cardiac rehabilitation programme that serves a city of 300,000 people and a large rural area. Since January 2023 patients referred after a heart attack, a stent or bypass surgery can choose our usual eight-week centre-based programme (two supervised exercise and education sessions a week) or a remote programme with the same content delivered at home, with a weekly video or telephone coaching call and a step counter. About 38 percent now choose remote. The board is asking whether remote rehabilitation should become the default, and staff are split: some think remote patients drop out quietly, others think the centre programme loses the people who live furthest away or cannot leave work.

We have programme records for every referral from January 2023 to December 2025: referral date, diagnosis, age, sex, postcode, which programme was chosen, sessions attended or coaching weeks completed, and the six-minute walk distance at the start and at the end for those who finished. I would like to do a retrospective comparison of completion between the two programmes, defining completion as attending at least 12 of 16 sessions or completing at least 6 of 8 coaching weeks, and to see whether any difference holds for women, older people and people living in deprived or remote areas.

I know that patients chose their programme, so the groups differ, and I need advice on how to handle that honestly with the data we have, which outcomes beyond completion are worth reporting, and how many patients we need. Our analyst support is limited to about 30 hours, and I cannot collect any new data from patients.
inputs.constraints: Existing programme records only, January 2023 to December 2025; about 30 hours of analyst support; no new data collection from patients; results are needed for the board's service review in April 2027.
localFacts: The programme received 1,146 referrals between January 2023 and December 2025; 436 patients chose the remote programme.
The information governance office approved access to the rehabilitation programme records for this analysis on 2026-08-27 (approval IG-CR-2026-19).
The research ethics board granted a waiver of consent for secondary use of the programme records on 2026-09-15 (REB-2026-331).
Six-minute walk distance is recorded at the start of both programmes and at the end only for patients who finish.

records.title: Home-based versus centre-based cardiac rehabilitation: completion and exercise capacity in a regional service
records.authors: Lindberg-Asante M, Hollis-Nakamura R, Petrov-Achebe S
records.abstract: We compared completion and exercise capacity between patients who chose home-based and those who chose centre-based cardiac rehabilitation in one regional service over three years. Among 1,208 patients, completion was 74 percent in the home-based programme and 52 percent in the centre-based programme. Six-minute walk distance improved by a mean of 48 metres in both groups among patients who completed. Patients choosing home-based rehabilitation were younger, more often men and more often in paid work. Completion was defined differently for the two programmes, and patients who never started were counted differently.

records.title: Remote versus centre-based cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction: a randomised non-inferiority trial
records.abstract: We randomised 390 adults after myocardial infarction to remote rehabilitation with weekly coaching calls or to a centre-based programme of the same length. The primary outcome, change in six-minute walk distance at 12 weeks, was non-inferior for remote rehabilitation (mean difference minus 6 metres, within the margin of 25 metres). Completion was 80 percent in the remote group and 71 percent in the centre group. Participants were younger than the usual rehabilitation population, and people without a smartphone were excluded.

records.title: Home-based compared with centre-based cardiac rehabilitation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
records.authors: Varga-Pellegrini A, Holm-Mensah D, Iwata-Brooks C
records.abstract: We searched five databases for randomised trials comparing home-based and centre-based cardiac rehabilitation in adults after a cardiac event or revascularisation. In all, 23 trials with 2,890 participants were included. Mortality, exercise capacity and quality of life were similar between settings. Completion was slightly higher with home-based rehabilitation (risk ratio 1.04, 95 percent confidence interval 0.97 to 1.12). Trials mostly enrolled men under 65, and definitions of completion varied between trials. Few trials reported outcomes beyond 12 months, and none reported completion separately for women or for people living in deprived areas.

records.title: Who completes remote cardiac rehabilitation? Predictors of dropout in a digital programme
records.abstract: We examined dropout among 652 patients who chose a remote cardiac rehabilitation programme with a step counter and weekly calls. Overall, 31 percent dropped out before week six. Dropout was higher among women (odds ratio 1.42), patients aged 75 or over (odds ratio 1.67) and those living in the most deprived areas (odds ratio 1.58). Most dropout followed two missed coaching calls in a row. Patients who completed the first two weeks usually finished the programme. The programme did not record the reasons patients gave for stopping.

records.title: Travel distance and completion of centre-based cardiac rehabilitation in a rural region
records.abstract: We linked travel distance from home postcode to completion of centre-based cardiac rehabilitation for 1,034 patients in a rural region. Each additional 10 km of travel was associated with lower odds of completing the programme (odds ratio 0.91, 95 percent confidence interval 0.87 to 0.95). Patients living more than 40 km away completed in 38 percent of cases, compared with 63 percent of those within 10 km. Access to a car and employment status were not recorded. The authors suggest offering a remote or hybrid option to patients who live far from the centre.

records.title: Defining completion in cardiac rehabilitation: variation across programmes and its effect on reported rates
records.abstract: We applied six published definitions of completion to the same records of 2,214 patients from four cardiac rehabilitation programmes. Reported completion rates varied from 41 to 79 percent depending on the definition applied to the same records. Definitions based on a proportion of sessions attended gave higher rates than definitions requiring an end-of-programme assessment. Home-based and centre-based programmes were most comparable when both used attendance-equivalent measures over the same number of weeks. The authors recommend that comparisons between settings state the definition used and keep non-starters in every denominator.

records.title: Barriers to cardiac rehabilitation among women: a qualitative study
records.abstract: We held semi-structured interviews with 28 women who were referred to cardiac rehabilitation and did not complete it. Caring responsibilities, transport and feeling out of place in groups of older men were the main barriers. Several women said that a programme at home would have fitted around their caring, while others valued the social contact of a centre. Participants were recruited from one urban hospital and most were over 60. Women who had completed rehabilitation in the past described it as worthwhile once they had started.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Randomised evidence suggests that remote or home-based rehabilitation gives similar outcomes and similar or higher completion than centre-based programmes in younger, mostly male populations. Observational comparisons where patients choose their setting report larger differences, but completion rates depend heavily on the definition used (41 to 79 percent on the same records), travel distance lowers centre-based completion, and remote dropout is higher among women, older and more deprived patients.
response.gradeRationale: Randomised evidence is indirect for this population; the observational comparisons are confounded by choice and by inconsistent definitions of completion.

response.overview: Retrospective comparison of completion between remote and centre-based cardiac rehabilitation using programme records for all referrals from January 2023 to December 2025.

response.summary: One completion rule, full denominators and five pre-specified adjustment variables.

response.designSummary: Comparison of completion between two self-selected groups with adjustment and a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding.
response.sampleSize: The sample is all 1,146 referrals (436 remote, 710 centre). With completion near 60 percent, the standard error of the difference is about 3.0 percentage points (square root of 0.24/436 plus 0.24/710), so the study has 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 to detect a difference of about 8.3 percentage points, which the board regards as the smallest difference worth acting on. About 690 completers and 456 non-completers give more than 90 outcome events per adjustment variable.
response.primaryAnalysis: Adjusted risk difference and risk ratio for completion (remote against centre) from a log-binomial model, or a modified Poisson model if it fails to converge, with age, sex, diagnosis, deprivation quintile and road distance. The E-value for the risk ratio states how strong unmeasured confounding would need to be.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Completion by sex, age group (under 75, 75 or over), deprivation quintile and distance band with interaction tests reported as descriptive; weeks engaged by programme; walk distance change in completers without comparison; propensity-weighted estimate as a sensitivity analysis.
response.missingData: Postcode is missing for about 1 percent; those referrals are kept in the crude comparison and excluded from the adjusted one, and the numbers are reported.
response.multiplicity: One primary comparison; subgroup results are descriptive.
overfittingGuards: Five adjustment variables fixed in advance
response.summary: All 1,146 referrals give 80 percent power for about 8.3 points; one adjusted model with an E-value.

response.risks: Minimal: secondary use of programme records. The main risk is re-identification of patients in small rural subgroups, handled by suppressing cells under five.
response.consent: Waiver of consent granted for secondary use (REB-2026-331); a notice on the programme's web page explains the analysis and how to opt out.
response.data: Access under IG-CR-2026-19; postcodes are converted to deprivation quintile and distance and then deleted; the analysis file is pseudonymised and kept on the hospital research server.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: women, older people, people in deprived areas and rural patients are the groups most likely to be failed by either setting; completion and uptake are reported for each, and the board is told whether a remote default would leave any group worse off.
response.effectiveness: The comparison informs the default programme; it cannot show that remote rehabilitation causes higher or lower completion.
response.partnerships: Rehabilitation staff, the information governance office, and two patient partners (one who completed remotely, one who stopped).
response.rebPath: Research ethics board waiver of consent for secondary use (REB-2026-331) and information governance approval (IG-CR-2026-19) are both in place.
response.limitations: Confounding by choice; employment and car access unrecorded; one programme.
response.summary: Secondary use under a consent waiver, with small-cell suppression and equity reporting.

response.title: Completion of remote and centre-based cardiac rehabilitation: a retrospective comparison with a single completion definition
response.abstract: Objective: to compare completion between remote and centre-based cardiac rehabilitation when one definition and full denominators are used. Design: retrospective comparison of programme records for 1,146 referrals, 2023 to 2025. Analysis: adjusted risk difference with an E-value, and results by sex, age, deprivation and distance. Results and conclusions will follow the analysis.
response.introduction: Published comparisons of rehabilitation settings disagree, partly because completion is defined differently between programmes. A cited regional comparison has since been corrected by its authors, which is why the local analysis fixes one definition before extraction.
response.methods: All referrals who chose a programme are included, with non-starters in both denominators. Completion is 12 of 16 sessions or 6 of 8 coaching weeks. A log-binomial model adjusts for five referral factors.
response.results: No data have been analysed yet. The report will present uptake and completion by programme and by group, the adjusted difference and the E-value.
response.discussion: The discussion will weigh the adjusted difference against confounding by choice and state whether a remote default would leave any group worse off.
response.limitations: Confounding by choice; unrecorded employment and car access; one programme.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis; it will not claim that one setting causes better completion.
response.summary: STROBE and RECORD structured draft; the introduction notes the corrected source.
